(Saturday night through Thursday)
Issued at 233 AM EDT Fri Sep 11 2026

Easterly flow and high pressure will be two meteorological 
commonalities that we will continue to message into the foreseeable 
future. At the surface, erratically structured yet apparent Atlantic 
ridging will be the focal point behind our easterly wind late this 
weekend and at least into early next week. By Tuesday and beyond, 
models have been consistent in showing a strengthening of these 
surface easterlies as the aforementioned subtropical ridging shifts 
eastward toward the central subtropics far enough away from South 
Florida to lose its local influence. At the same time, anomalously 
strong surface ridging will work its way from west to east across 
the northern tier of the CONUS and toward New England and Atlantic 
Canada from late this weekend into upcoming work week. ECMWF 
ensemble data shows mean 1000-mb geopotential heights between the 
90th and 97th percentiles for climatology expanding well to the 
south and west of the primary ridge axis into the southwest Atlantic 
waters and just north of South Florida, which will help induce a 
stronger onshore flow across our region within the 5-7 day time 
frame. Coincident to this strong surface ridge will be an even more 
impressive upper-level anticyclonic pattern over the southeast/Mid- 
Atlantic US, where ECMWF ensemble forecasts are depicting 500-mb 
geopotential heights to be at the maximum percentiles for 
climatology through much of next week. With this abnormally strong 
feature overhead, we can expect any surface-based fronts and the 
overall storm track associated with the polar jet stream to stay 
well displaced to our north over the northern United States.

All the while, we are also monitoring evolving deterministic model 
trends with respect to the potential intrusion of Saharan dust 
during the latter half of the weekend and into next week, but mainly 
next week. NASA GEOS Dust Extinction Aerosol forecast shows a deep 
Saharan Air Layer (SAL) approaching the nearshore waters of South 
Florida on Sunday, but mostly staying to our south over the Keys and 
Florida Straits because of the aforementioned record-strong ridging 
aloft over the SE CONUS. It is not until Tuesday that models start 
to become a little more insistent on this dust actually penetrating 
our atmospheric column, with the NBM showing a reduction in PWATs to 
at or just below 2" (roughly between the 50th and 70th percentiles) 
on days 5-7 and forecast soundings displaying larger dew points 
depressions.

As we wrap up the weekend and head into the following work week 
preceding the arrival of the SAL, PWATs are forecast to remain 
generally within the 2.0-2.3" range (80th-95th percentiles) across 
South Florida which, in addition to abundant surface-based CAPE 
during each diurnal cycle and the easterly flow regime we will have 
in place, will continue to support the development of scattered to 
numerous showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and early 
evening hours with the highest coverage forecast to be over the 
western half of the peninsula. Main concerns will be dangerous cloud-
to-ground lighting, gusty and erratic winds, and heavy rainfall that 
could lead to localized flooding in and around the Naples metro with 
the impending Gulf sea breeze pushing inland every afternoon and 
working to counteract our prevailing easterly flow. PoPs are lowered 
for the latter half of this long-term forecast from Tuesday and 
beyond with the potential intrusion of Saharan dust, to which the 
extent of regional shower and thunderstorm coverage across South 
Florida is still to be determined.

Typical South Florida heat sticks around through the upcoming 
weekend and into next week, with highs consistently reaching the low 
to mid 90s each afternoon and maximum apparent/feels-like 
temperatures in the 100-105F range (with isolated higher values of 
106-107F). Make sure to take the proper precautions to protect 
yourself and those around you from these elevated temperatures, 
especially if spending extended periods of time outdoors.
